p.t: In short
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: **Google Ads shows paid ads to people who are already searching for what you sell.**
You pay **per click**. A better Quality Score (Google's rating of how relevant and clickable your ad is) lowers what each click costs.
For dropshipping (selling products that a supplier ships to your customer), **Shopping ads** are the main format.

If few people click your ad, **fix the ad** before you raise your bids.
Use Google Ads as **one** traffic source, not the only one.
Google Shopping puts your product next to the same product from other sellers. Price, title, shop name, reviews and delivery decide who gets the click.
Google works best for products people already search for. It fits expensive products best, roughly 1,000 USD and up.
Start with Google Ads only if the product already sells somewhere else or people already search for it. Test small first.
Do not follow Google's advice without checking it. Its suggestions usually ask you to spend more.
Check your competitors and their prices in the country you sell to before you launch.
Google Ads is usually the **steadier paid channel** than Facebook or TikTok, but it takes time to learn.

Your ad's position and cost depend on your bid and your Quality Score (Google's rating of how relevant your ad is). Raising your CTR (click-through rate, the share of viewers who click) is the first fix.
Start with **Shopping ads** and retargeting (showing ads again to people who already visited). Plain search ads come later, once your data supports them.

Judge an ad by the visitors it brings and whether they buy, not by the ad alone.
Do not pay an outside agency until your own ads are profitable.
Definition and Scope
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google Ads is a customizable, self-serve advertising platform. Self-serve means you set it up and run it yourself.
It includes search ads and the Google Display Network, a large group of partner websites, apps and videos where ads can appear.
The Display Network reaches **many** internet users beyond search results.
It is a pay-per-placement platform. Advertisers bid to show text, banners, videos, product listings or app install promotions.
A store owner pays to be seen by people who are already searching for or browsing related products.
Pay-per-click (PPC) means the advertiser pays **each time a user clicks** an ad.
PPC is the paid format used for search and shopping campaigns. A campaign is a group of ads with its own goal and budget.
Google Ads reaches people who are **actively searching** for solutions.
So it taps existing demand (people who already want something) rather than creating awareness.

It places you where people are already looking for what you sell.
The core of Google Ads is showing **the right ad** to the right person at the right time.

Getting these three elements right puts an advertiser well ahead of competitors.
Google Ads gives complete cost transparency, meaning you can see clearly what you spend.

You can see how much revenue each campaign generates.
This gives you full control of spending and profitability. Profitability means whether you make money after all costs.
Google Ads fits this model because **spend per sale is small** compared to the product price.
It can work for any product. It works best when the product's margin (the money left after the product cost) covers the ad budget.
Channels, campaign types and targeting
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
Google Ads serves on **three** main channels.
Channel 1: text search results on Google search.
Channel 2: Product Listing Ads (PLA, ads that show a product photo and price) through your Merchant Center (Google's account that holds your product data), using your Google Shopping data.
Channel 3: the Google Display Network, including YouTube, Gmail and many other sites.
Campaign types include **Shopping** Campaigns, Search Campaigns, Video Campaigns and campaigns on the Google Display Network.
Eight targeting options (ways to choose who sees your ad) are available.
The eight are: keywords for search (the words a user types); website and placement targeting for display; demographics; audience interests and life events; topics; YouTube videos and channels;

customer match; and remarketing (showing ads again to people who already visited).
The four Google traffic methods (ways visitors reach your store) work as **one** integrated system.

Organic search provides free, high-intent traffic. High intent means the visitor is close to buying.
Product listings add free visibility.

Shopping ads deliver scalable paid traffic with maximum control.
Remarketing recaptures interested visitors who did not buy.

Google Organic Search is free traffic from visitors who click non-paid text search results.
Most clicks concentrate on the **first page** of Google results.

Google Ads is one traffic source among several, never the only one.
Once the account is running, the next step is to **add other marketing channels**.

Google Ads should not be the only channel.
Use it as the starting point. Get campaigns running and producing results.
Then add other traffic channels that complement the Google Ads account.
Verify that all components of the traffic system are complete and live (live means public and working):

1. Google Search Console (Google's free tool that shows how Google sees your site) set up and verified
2. Google Merchant Center approved

3. Products submitted correctly to Merchant Center
4. Shopping ads campaign created
5. Remarketing campaign live
The Auction
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google Ads runs an auction (a contest between advertisers) for **every search query** (the words a user types).
Advertisers place bids (the price they offer per click) to have their ads shown for specific queries.
Competing advertisers bid on the same queries at the same time.
The auction decides the order of ads on the results page: which ad appears first, second, third and so on.
Ads are ranked for each query individually. The same advertiser can hold different positions for different queries.
Google decides which search terms your ads are eligible for, based on the **product data** you supply.
Google's auction is a second-price auction, not a typical auction where the highest bidder pays their own bid.

The winning advertiser pays **just above** the next competitor's ranking.
It does not pay the full amount of its own maximum bid.
The standard cost-per-click (CPC, what you pay for one click) formula for the second-price auction uses Ad Rank (your position score, which is your bid times your Quality Score).
actual cost per click = (Ad Rank of the advertiser directly below you ÷ your Quality Score) + $0.01 Ad Rank = maximum bid × Quality Score
A higher Quality Score lowers the price you pay for the same position.
Approximate cost per click: take the Ad Rank of the bidder directly below you, divide by your own Quality Score, then add **$0.01**.
You never pay more than your maximum bid. The actual price depends on the competitors around you.
Worked example: the bidder with Ad Rank 32 sits below a bidder with Quality Score 10, giving 32 / 10 + $0.01 = $3.21 per click.

Do not assume you pay your full bid per click, as you would at a house or product auction.
Your actual cost depends on the competitor below you and your Quality Score.
So a high bid with a low Quality Score can still cost more per click than necessary.
Ad rank and position
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Ad Rank = maximum bid × Quality Score.
The highest Ad Rank takes the top position. A bidder with a strong Quality Score can outrank a higher bidder.

Google earns money when people **click** ads, not when they buy on the advertiser's site.
For this reason, it rewards ads that people want to click with a higher Quality Score.
A higher ad position brings more traffic than a lower one, regardless of competitors.

A bidder with a well-optimized Quality Score can therefore get more clicks while bidding **less** than the competition.
Google and Facebook prefer ads that get clicked.
So they reward advertisers whose ads perform well with cheaper clicks. Their quality metrics exist to enforce this.
Google Ads uses Quality Score, Facebook uses Relevance Score, and Amazon also uses a quality score.

All three measure how well an ad matches what people want and how often they click it.
A bidder with a very low Quality Score can have the **highest bid** and still rank low.

A bidder who bids too little with a strong Quality Score can miss the top results entirely.
Ad rank historically combined the bid with a bundle of factors known as Quality Score.

A competitor with a higher Quality Score can rank above you with a lower bid.
A lower Quality Score forces you to bid much higher to move up.
Ad rank and Quality Score cannot be measured directly in the Google Ads interface.
Any change to them has to be **tested** and judged from indirect results, because no one knows the exact outcome.

Bids and Quality Scores in this example:
**Bidder A**
Max bid: $3.75

Quality Score: 10
Ad Rank (bid x QS): 37.5
Position: 1
**Bidder B**
Max bid: $4.00

Quality Score: 8
Ad Rank (bid x QS): 32
Position: 2
**Bidder C**
Max bid: $3.45

Quality Score: 7
Ad Rank (bid x QS): 24.15
Position: 3
**Bidder D**
Max bid: not stated

Quality Score: 6
Ad Rank (bid x QS): not stated
Position: 4
**Bidder E**
Max bid: $5.00
Worked auction example (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
Quality Score: 3
Ad Rank (bid x QS): 15
Position: 5
**Bidder F**
Max bid: $2.50

Quality Score: 4
Ad Rank (bid x QS): 10
Position: 6
**Bidder G**
Max bid: $1.70

Quality Score: 5
Ad Rank (bid x QS): 8.50
Position: not stated
**Bidder H**
Max bid: $0.50

Quality Score: high
Ad Rank (bid x QS): high
Position: first page
Bidder A ranks above Bidder B **despite bidding $0.25 less**.
Bidder E bids the most but ranks fifth because of its very low Quality Score.

A high Quality Score gives **discounted clicks**.
A low Quality Score triggers a penalty that raises the cost per click.
p.h: Cost per click and click quality

p.t:
So Quality Score changes what you pay, not only where your ad shows.
Quality Score affects ad rank, not only the price paid.

In the example, a bidder with the highest bid but a low Quality Score was not shown.
A bidder with a lower bid and the strongest Quality Score took the top position.

A high Quality Score lets an advertiser win placement with a **smaller bid**.
Moving from a Quality Score of 5 to 6 gave about a **16%** CPC discount.

Moving from 5 to 7 gave about a **30%** discount.
When Quality Score rises, CPC falls.

So an advertiser with a higher score can bid low and still appear first and receive the most clicks.
Bidding high is not required to win top placement.
Shopping ads charge per click.

Cost-per-click is lowered when your ad gets a **higher click-through rate** (CTR, the share of people who see your ad and click it) and visitors stay longer on your site than on competitors' sites. (2023)
Google evaluates post-click behavior on the store: bounce rate (visitors who leave right away), time on site, add-to-cart (putting an item in the basket) and purchase. (2024)
Strong engagement raises Quality Score and lets ads show more for less. (2024)
So the conversion tag (a small code that reports sales back to Google) must be set up for tracking. (2024)

Shopping ads show the price in the ad, so shoppers who object to the price do not click.
This filters out unqualified clicks before they cost money.
Quality Score
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Quality Score is Google's rating of how relevant your ads and landing pages are to a search query.

A landing page is the page a visitor arrives on after clicking.
It is based on expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing page experience.
It affects both the price you pay per click and how competitive your ad is against others for the same query.

Quality Score in Google Ads is based on how relevant the ad is to the searched term.
It also depends on how often people click the ad.

It also depends on whether visitors stay on the landing page instead of leaving immediately.
A high score lets an advertiser rank well without outbidding everyone.
Quality Score depends largely on **click-through rate**, along with landing page quality and site experience.

Advertisers with a higher Quality Score compete better in the auction.
At equal bids they usually pay less per click within a certain range.

A slow website can lower Quality Score through the on-page experience factor.
Search text ads once showed per-keyword quality breakdowns.

Shopping never showed these breakdowns, though the same factors still apply.
Google does not publish the exact Ad Rank or Quality Score factors or their weights.

The bid is the main lever for search impression share (how often your ad shows out of all the times it could show).
Quality Score factors help make your bid more competitive.

Google Shopping uses its own algorithm (set of calculation rules), separate from search.
Google Ads shows Quality Score **per keyword**, with change history.
It does not show a Quality Score column for Shopping campaigns.
Google has no separate advertiser-level Quality Score visible to the advertiser. Only the keyword level is displayed.

Improving an existing campaign is generally **better than creating a new one**.
Campaign history and steady spend help the account.
CTR as the main lever
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google measures whether people like an ad mainly through Click-Through Rate (CTR).

A high CTR is the main signal of a clickable ad.
CTR = Clicks ÷ Impressions (impressions are the number of times your ad was shown).

A higher CTR increases Quality Score and lowers CPC.
So a higher CTR gives cheaper clicks.
CTR has the largest influence on Quality Score.

If your CTR is **below the benchmark**, you probably have a Quality Score problem.
Google measures relevance through click-through rate.

A low CTR, where people see the ad but do not click, lowers ad rank.
Google reads it as weak relevance compared with competitors.

Most paid-traffic problems can be traced back to CTR.
So **start diagnosis there**.

For Shopping, the two ad types worth optimizing most are ad engagement and Shopping campaign CTR.
These are the two levers to address first.

When an account has high bids but almost no traffic, the usual cause is that the ads are not clickable.
It is not that the bids are too low.

So **fix ad quality before raising bids**.
Raising CTR, which drives Quality Score, is therefore the main lever for cheaper clicks.
Google does not show a Quality Score column for Shopping campaigns.
Use the Benchmark CTR, which reflects the **average CTR** of competing advertisers, to estimate the Shopping Quality Score.

If your CTR is below the Benchmark CTR, a Quality Score problem is likely.
Bidding more will not fix it.

In the example, the advertiser had a 0.77% CTR against a 0.94% benchmark.
So competitors were paying less per click for the same visibility.
Google shows an ad in more than one position for a query when the ad's CTR is higher than the average for that position.

Each position has an average CTR.
An ad that beats its position average gets moved up.
Moving up then makes its CTR even higher.
Funnel Position: Funnel Model
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: The sales funnel is an inverse pyramid (wide at the top, narrow at the bottom).
It has TOFU (top of funnel, awareness stage), MOFU (middle of funnel, consideration stage) and BoFU (bottom of funnel, buying stage).

Going down the funnel, audience size **declines** but purchase intent increases.
Apply this framework when structuring Google Ads campaigns.

The funnel runs Awareness, Interest, Learn, Shop, Buy.
Google Ads works well because its campaigns target people at the bottom of the funnel who are ready to buy.

The goal is to reach only those at the Buy stage.
Do not target people who are only researching or aware of a product.

Paid traffic works when the right ad reaches the right customer at the right stage of the funnel.
Most people at the top are only researching.

A larger group is comparing options.
Only a **small share** at the bottom is ready to buy now.
Funnel-aligned spending is more effective and profitable.

BoFU audiences have much higher conversion rates (the share of visitors who buy).
They require less budget to generate sales than spending on TOFU awareness audiences.
Intent maps onto the sales funnel. Low-value terms sit at the top, medium at the middle and high at the bottom.
Google Shopping and search text ads perform best in the middle and bottom of the funnel.
They perform poorly for high-ticket products at the top. High-ticket means expensive products.
Match each funnel stage with a different ad message.
At the top, reach people who are unaware of the product or the problem with informational content.
In the middle, serve people comparing options with webinars, buying guides, comparison guides and detailed video reviews.

At the bottom, show direct product ads to people who are **ready to buy**.
No tool currently matches the right ad to each funnel stage automatically.
So audience and ad segmentation (splitting people into groups) by funnel stage has to be planned and set up manually.
Where Google sits in the funnel
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google Ads is excellent for middle and bottom funnel work, such as retargeting previous visitors.
It is weak for top funnel because it cannot reach cold audiences (people unaware of the product).
Google is mostly a bottom-of-funnel platform. Its search and shopping ads are triggered by product searches.

Top-of-funnel testing should be done on Facebook and TikTok **first**.
Test on Google once the product works with branded content.

Google Ads cannot interrupt journeys or show new products to cold audiences.
It works best where people already search for solutions or have pre-existing intent.
Google Shopping works best for middle and bottom of the funnel. These are shoppers already searching for specific products.

It performs poorly for high-ticket businesses at the top of the funnel.
Spending heavily on top-of-funnel traffic makes the campaign unprofitable.

Google Ads are strong in the middle and bottom of the funnel but weak at the top.
Social media is strong at the top, and YouTube works across the whole funnel.

Using them together gives full coverage of the customer journey.
Google is strong for retargeting and for buyers who search for the product.
Cold traffic from Google is **less scalable** than Facebook, because customers must already be searching for the product.
Use Google to reach people with search intent rather than to find new audiences.
Target Google Ads at search queries with a high chance of leading to a sale rather than broad interest.
Expensive products should not be pushed to cold audiences on social media in the first phase.
Cold traffic from Google includes Google Shopping, Google display ads, Google search text ads and YouTube ads.
Google and Bing are the main channels for front-end demand on expensive products, since they reach people already searching.

Facebook and Instagram are better suited to remarketing.
Most high-ticket sales come from Google Shopping ads and organic search.

This is because buyers of expensive items use search engines.
Social media is not a main channel in this model. It is used only for retargeting.

Google Shopping reaches people who are **actively searching** for a specific product.
Social media reaches people who are mostly not ready to buy.
For expensive products, this makes search-based traffic more likely to convert.
Ad types and placements: Overview of Types
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Four main Google Ads types matter for a dropshipping store: Search Text Ads, Display Ads, YouTube Ads

and Shopping Ads.
Other ad types exist but are rarely used in this approach.
Google Ads shows ads in several placements (places where ads appear).
These are search results (SERP, the page of results after a search), Shopping (including on mobile), the Display Network on individual websites, Gmail and YouTube.
For e-commerce, search and Shopping placements usually deserve the **most attention first**.

Google Ads and Bing Ads are paid search channels. They show ads to people actively searching for products.
Use them as main paid traffic sources next to Facebook Ads.
Search Text Ads appear at the top of Google search results for a keyword (the word or phrase you bid on), marked as paid.

They are won through a keyword auction where the highest bidder ranks first.
Bid amount alone does not decide position, because Quality Score also counts.
Google search text ads are the sponsored ads that appear above the organic results. Organic results are the free, unpaid listings.

Search text ads can outperform Shopping in some cases, especially outside the US.
So **test both formats** before deciding.

On a results page, Shopping ads come first.
Then comes the first block of search text ads, then organic results, then a second block of text ads at the bottom.

Shopping results are shown above all other ads when Google has relevant products.
When relevant Shopping ads exist for a search, they are the first results a shopper sees.

They appear above search text ads and organic results.
On desktop they sit at the top of the page, above the fold (the part visible without scrolling).
Google shows no further Shopping ads lower on the page, only search text ads.
Shopping Ads
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Shopping Ads show a product image, product name, price, store URL and a short description for matching searches.
They work very well for dropshipping stores and are a core part of the approach.
Google Shopping ads are paid placements that show the product image, store name and price.

They appear at the front of Google and at the top of the Google Shopping section.
This makes them the most controllable traffic source in this method set.

Google Shopping ads appear in a carousel (a sliding row) at the top of the regular Google results page for product searches.
They also appear in the Shopping tab.

They are labeled "Sponsored products" and are charged per click.
Shopping ads display the product image, price and product name directly in the ad.

The user sees exactly what they would be clicking.
This makes these clicks purchase-ready, which is why they tend to convert better than generic ads.
Shopping ads were reported to convert about **30% better** than standard text ads.
They were also reported to produce about **40% higher** average order value (the average amount spent per order).
In the same source, Shopping ads made up about 60% of Google ad clicks.
They made up about 82% of non-branded clicks. (Non-branded clicks are clicks from searches that do not use a brand name.)
For high-ticket dropshipping, Google Shopping produces **most** of the sales that come from Google Ads traffic.

This holds for about 90% of businesses, usually at the best profitability.
Some stores, especially outside the US, get better results from search text ads.
Shopping Ads (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
So test both formats before deciding.
Google Shopping is the main Google Ads format for high-ticket dropshipping.
For most such businesses it generates the majority of ad-driven sales at the best profitability.

Search text ads can outperform it in some cases, especially outside the US.
The Display Network is a secondary format.

Shopping ads appear at the top of the results page, where most clicks and sales come from.
Free product listings appear lower and require submission to Google Merchant Center.

Google Shopping ads are the first traffic source for a new store.
They bring in shoppers with clear purchase intent.

Facebook ads should follow to re-engage visitors who leave the site.
Google Shopping is the highest converting traffic source for these stores.
Keep it as the core of paid traffic and focus optimization effort there.

Start conversion work with Google Shopping campaigns, since they usually bring most of a store's traffic.
Only then move to remarketing.

Judge those campaigns by their own conversion rate, not the store-wide average.
Google Shopping product listing ads are a main traffic source.
They send shoppers directly to a product page on the Shopify store.
Shopping ads appear in Google's Shopping tab and in regular search results.
This happens when a user searches for a brand name, product name or SKU (stock keeping unit, a product's internal code) that exists in the product feed (the product data file you send to Google).

Merchant Center must hold the products.
Merchant Center must also be linked to the Google Ads account before any of this works.
Product Listing Ads (PLA)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Product listing ads (PLAs) are image-based product ads shown in Google search results.

They display a product image, title, price, store name and star ratings.
This gives shoppers a lot of buying information before they click.

Google Product Listing Ads show products with images and prices directly in Google search results.
They are one of the main traffic sources in this model.

PLAs reach people who are already searching for a product.
Facebook ads, by contrast, interrupt users who are browsing their feed without buying intent.
This makes PLAs a stronger fit for buyers than interruption-based placements.
Until a store makes more than **$50,000 in sales per month**, keep focusing the paid budget on Google Product Listing Ads. Do not start other paid channels.

Google PLAs stay in use even after that point.
But they are no longer the only focus.

PLAs only appear for commercial search queries, meaning searches where the user is looking to buy.
Informational how-to queries show few or no product ads.

This filters out clicks from people who are not interested in buying.
With Shopping campaigns you do not select keywords yourself.

Google decides which searches trigger your product ads.
It does this mainly by matching the search against your product data, especially product titles.

Google automatically classifies each search as commercial or non-commercial.
It only shows product ads for the commercial ones.

This classification happens **without any keyword setup** from the advertiser.
A commercial search such as "infrared sauna" showed many product listing ads.
The informational search "how to install cabinet doors" showed only one product ad next to a knowledge panel (an info box with facts).
The difference shows how Google separates buying intent from research intent.
The Google Display Network places image banners of various sizes on partner websites across the internet.
For a new store with a small budget, Display Ads usually have a weak return on ad spend (ROAS, the money earned per money spent on ads).

They are **not recommended** as a starting point.
They become more useful as the business grows.
Google Ads serves on the Google Display Network, which includes YouTube, Gmail and many other sites.
YouTube
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
YouTube Ads appear before or during videos on YouTube.
Viewers can skip after **5 seconds**.

They need extra production work to set up.
They usually give a weaker return on ad spend than other Google ad types.

So they are not recommended for beginners.
YouTube works across the whole funnel, so it is useful at every stage when combined with other channels.
Besides brand search, other Google campaign types include dynamic ads and Smart Shopping campaigns.
Performance Max (an automated campaign type that mixes channels) is treated as the **second priority** after a brand search campaign.
Google Ads campaign types include Shopping Campaigns, Search Campaigns, Video Campaigns and Display Network campaigns.
Google search results show Shopping ads in the right-hand column and text search ads on the left.
Shopping also appears on mobile, where Shopping Spotlight ads present products in a richer format.

For e-commerce, Shopping placements often need the **most attention**.
Google changes how Shopping results are displayed over time.

For example, they may appear as a horizontal row at the top or a vertical block on the side.
A different layout on a later check is normal. It is not a reason to change the campaign.

Shopping ads appear mainly on the Google search results page.
They can also show on other Google properties such as YouTube video overlays and Gmail inboxes.

Placement settings control where they run.
Shopping ads appear mainly on the Google search results page.

They can also show as overlays on YouTube videos and in Gmail inboxes.
On desktop they sit above the fold.

Google may change their layout at any time.
Shoppers can click the Shopping tab on the results page to see a larger grid of related products.
Clicking a product ad sends the shopper directly to the retailer's product page.

Shopping ads always send traffic to the product page of the promoted item, not to collection pages.
This is the default behavior and **cannot be changed**.
How Google Shopping works (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: How Google Shopping works
Google Shopping works as a comparison shopping engine. It is a search site that lists the same product from many sellers so buyers can compare them.

Shoppers compare the same or similar products by **price**, title, shop name, reviews and delivery.
They do this **without opening each site**.

Your product page is judged directly against the competitors shown beside it.
Customers compare the same product across several retailers.
They look at **price**, brand, delivery, special offers, reviews and seller.
As a reseller (a shop that sells products it did not make), you are always compared directly with other sellers of the same product.

Google Shopping is a comparison engine by design.
You **cannot** avoid comparison with other sellers of the same product inside it.

If you cannot accept competing with identical listings, this channel is not a good fit.
Shoppers decide mainly on **price**, product title, retailer name and reviews.
When five or more shops sell the same product, the listing also shows delivery and special offers.

Shoppers decide on price, product title, retailer name and reviews.
They may also see delivery and special offers when several shops are listed.

Shopping ads place your product next to other sellers' near-identical listings.
This makes price competition a **race to the bottom**: prices keep falling until profit is gone.

Differentiate with better offers, better content and better images, not with price.
Do not compete against the AliExpress listing itself.

Google Shopping only shows "compare prices at X stores" when **multiple sellers** list the same product.
If only one listing exists, only one price appears. (2024)
Shared product pages
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: A shared product page is one Google page where several sellers' offers for the same item are grouped.

When several retailers sell the same product, Google groups their listings together.
The price range can be **wide**.
A listing marked as refurbished (used or repaired, but sold as like-new) can show the lowest price.
Check the condition label when you benchmark competitors (compare your prices and offers with theirs).

Google groups listings with matching product data onto one shared product page.
Matching data includes the same **GTIN** (a product's barcode number) and brand.

Each seller shows its own price, delivery and offers on that page.
Resellers of the same item therefore compete on that page.

Price, delivery and offer details decide which seller gets the click.
A seller can list a refurbished unit under the same identifiers (product codes such as GTIN).

That seller can appear with the **lowest price** on the shared product page.
The condition is only visible in the details.

A retailer that sells only new products must expect such lower prices.
It must compete on other factors: delivery, offers and page clarity.
A query is what a customer types into search.
For each search, Google checks whether the seller's product feed contains a matching product.

A product feed is a file that lists your products and their details, sent to Google.
If there is a match, Google runs an auction among the retailers who submitted that product.

An auction here is a quick contest between sellers for one click.
Entry depends on three things: the **bid**, enough budget to win a click, and negative keywords.

A bid is the most you will pay for one click.
A budget is the money you allow for your ads.

Negative keywords are search words that stop your ad from showing.
Google Shopping entry procedure, as described in the source:

1. A customer enters a **search** on Google.
2. Google checks whether a product in the merchant's (seller's) product feed can match that search.
Query matching and auction entry (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: 3. If there is a match, Google runs an **auction** among eligible retailers, considering each one's bid, budget and negative keywords.
4. If the bid and budget win the auction and no negative keyword blocks the search, the Shopping ad is generated and shown to the customer.

Google wants to show ads for many searches that have some chance of a sale.
It does **not** filter by intent (what the shopper really wants to buy).

You must build the filtering yourself with bids, budgets and negative keywords.
Avoid too much low-value traffic that uses up your budget.

Google matches your products to a broad range of search terms.
Most of its revenue comes from ads.
It accepts loosely related searches as long as some sale chance exists.
So you must manage **intent-based bidding** (bidding more for searches that show buying intent) and exclusions (blocking searches you do not want).
Search results and ad details depend on the searcher's location.

Check how your ads look from the **target country** (the country you sell to) before you judge them.
Local tax and delivery display are part of that check.
In the US, Google can show a **sales tax** column per state. Sales tax is a tax added to the price.
That column is based on the shopper's IP address location (the number that shows where a device connects).

In Australia, the single national GST of **10%** is included in the displayed price. GST means Goods and Services Tax.
It is not shown as a separate column.

Some markets show sales tax as a separate column.
That column is based on the shopper's IP location.

In Australia, tax is included in the price and not shown separately.
The reason: the national rate is a single **10%**.
When Google suits a product or store
Product Fit
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google Ads works best for products where people already search for solutions.

This is called pre-existing intent: shoppers already want what you sell.
Examples: furniture, health and fitness.
Furniture and home decor are good categories for Google Ads.
They are **high-ticket** products (expensive items, roughly 1,000 USD and up) with good search volume (how many people search a term each month).

Allow **one to two weeks** to warm up the account.
Warming up means letting the account collect data, so Google's automatic system (the algorithm) learns the audience.

For Google ads for clothing, **collection and catalogue ads** perform best.
These are ads that show several related products together.

For high-ticket products, **Google Search and Google Shopping** are the main paid channels to start with.
A paid channel is a place where you pay for ads.
Buyers of expensive items look for solutions via search engines, not on social platforms like Facebook, Instagram or Pinterest.
For high-ticket e-commerce products, Google Ads (search and Shopping) and **organic SEO** are the main marketing channels.
Organic means free results, and SEO (search engine optimization) means improving your site so it ranks in those free results.
Buyers with a question or problem type it into a search engine.
So search is where you meet them, not social feeds where they are not actively looking for such products.
Google Shopping campaigns for expensive products need a **different structure** than campaigns for low-priced items.

A campaign is a group of ads with its own budget and settings.
Low-priced examples: deodorant, toothbrushes or 30 USD t-shirts.

Follow the high-ticket approach step by step.
Do not apply generic low-ticket setups.
Google Shopping campaigns for high-ticket dropshipping need a **more advanced setup** than basic campaigns.
Product Fit (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Dropshipping means you sell items that a supplier ships directly to the customer, so you never hold the stock yourself.
Expect the setup and ongoing management to take more time to learn.

A good traffic source combines three things: traffic volume, affordable cost per visitor, and a good chance of conversion.
Conversion means a visitor who buys.

Google Ads is a suitable starting point because it offers all three together.
Google Shopping is a sensible first traffic source for a new high-ticket store.
It reaches people who are already searching for the product. (see next subsection for conflicting views)
For a new high-ticket dropshipping store, paid Google Ads and Google Shopping are a sensible first traffic source.

They deliver traffic **almost immediately**.
Organic search traffic takes much longer to build.

Paid search ads can be switched on immediately and bring traffic **within a day**.
SEO typically needs **several months** before measurable results appear.

Paid ads suit the early launch phase of a new store.
They should not be the only traffic source over time.
Early paid traffic lets a new store collect **performance data**, customer feedback and customer service experience.

These show what buyers want, what they reject, and whether the website fits the market.
Start paid traffic with Google Ads before other paid channels.
The reason: the supply of qualified shoppers (people likely to buy) on Google Ads is large enough to justify mastering it first.
Google Ads works best for a store that already gets roughly **1,000 to 5,000** monthly site visitors.
It also needs Google Analytics (a free tool that counts visitors) and the pixel (a small tracking code on your site) connected.

Without existing traffic and tracking, Google campaigns have little data to learn from.
Google Ads for drop shipping does not make sense as a **first test**.
Store readiness and timing (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google is expensive at the top of the funnel (the early stage, when people first notice a product).

Use it only once the product is proven and you have a branded store (a store with its own name and identity).
Then it is a good source of conversions.

Google Ads is suitable for beginners only in two cases.
Case one: the product already generates sales (proof of concept, meaning proof it works) on another platform.

Case two: the product has inherent search intent, so people already search for it.
Revenue from Google Ads differs strongly by market.

Some high-ticket stores make **multiple millions of dollars** per year from Google Ads alone.
In other markets, the same channel may make only about **$500,000** per year.
The sources disagree on whether Google should be the first paid channel. Each applies under different conditions:

Google Shopping as the first traffic source for a new store, with Facebook following to re-engage visitors (bring back people who left the site).
Source from 2019, so older.

Applies to a new store with clear purchase intent.
Keep the paid budget on Google PLAs (Product Listing Ads, the image-and-price ads in Google Shopping).

Do not start other paid channels until the store makes more than **$50,000** in sales per month.
Source from 2018, so older.
Applies below that sales level.

Google Ads and Google Shopping as a sensible first source for a new high-ticket store, because traffic arrives almost immediately.
Source from 2021-22, so older.

Applies to high-ticket products with search demand.
Google as a later step, not a first test, because it is expensive at the top of the funnel.
Applies to drop-shipping products that have not been proven and have no branded store.

Google as a beginner channel only when the product already sells elsewhere or has inherent search intent.
Applies to beginners.

Test top-of-funnel (early awareness) on Facebook and TikTok first.
Test on Google once the product works with branded content.
Applies to products that need awareness testing.
Scaling and Competition
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: A single product on Google Ads has a scaling ceiling based on search volume and user intent.

Scaling means spending more to grow sales. A ceiling is the upper limit.
Scaling depends on how much search demand exists.
Unlike Meta (Facebook and Instagram) or TikTok, where account capacity allows higher scaling.

An established competitor's edge in paid Shopping comes from better-optimized campaigns with more data.
It usually comes from **higher bids**, not from store age.
A new store can match or outrank them quickly in paid results by optimizing its campaigns and bidding more.

Competition in Google Shopping is measured **per product**, not per store.
Count the stores that sell the same specific product.
Do not count the total number of stores in the niche (a narrow market segment). (2024)
If more than **10 suppliers** advertise the most popular product in Google Shopping, do not bid on that product with Shopping ads.

Rely on free organic listings and traffic instead.
Google Ads is well suited to this model.

The reason: spend per sale is small compared with the product price.
Google Ads has been the most profitable traffic source across niches for over a decade.

So do not abandon it after weak early results.
Refine campaigns before moving to other channels.
Procedure for a target country:
p.h: Competitor check before launching Google Shopping

p.t: 1. Connect a VPN (a tool that makes your connection look like it comes from another country) with an IP address from the **target country**.

2. Search the **product name** on Google.
3. Open the Shopping listings of competitors.

4. Compare their images, pricing, free shipping tags and whether they look unique or high quality.
5. Create a **stronger first image** if competitors look generic.
Control and Automation
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: The main advantage of paid traffic is **control over who sees an ad**.
Targeting can use demographics (basic facts about people, such as age), household income, search behavior and other signals.

A billboard reaches a broad crowd.
It makes it hard to tell which exposures led to a sale.
Targeted paid ads can be measured and adjusted.
Google Ads gives you control over where and when your ads appear.
When you evaluate new features or options, be skeptical of anything that removes your control.

Such features trade away the ability to target the right audiences precisely.
They also put visibility ahead of conversions (sales).

Avoid Google Ads features that take away control over bidding, targeting or ad creation.
They tend to optimize for visibility rather than direct conversions.
Google's former AdWords Express (an older, fully automated setup) bundled automated bidding, automated targeting and automated ad creation.

It is the example of this kind of setup to avoid.
Creating a campaign without goals guidance (Google's guided goal setup) gives more manual control over settings.
More control over campaigns tends to produce a higher **return on ad spend** (ROAS: sales you get back for each dollar spent) than letting Google automate by fitting into its boxes.
Google's Shopping campaign setup has changed little in about a decade.
Google does not publish how **ad rank** (Google's score that sets your ad position) or **Quality Score** (Google's rating of ad and keyword quality) work.
Be skeptical of anyone claiming hidden shortcuts.
Once the known levers (settings you can control) are handled, further account optimization usually brings **diminishing returns** (smaller and smaller gains).
Interface-Change Mindset
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google Ads makes significant changes **almost monthly**.
It requires regular monitoring of the official Google Ads Blog, Google Ads Updates and Google Ads Support to maintain campaign performance.
The core rule for Google Ads campaigns stays the same: right message, right person, right time.

This rule stays valid whatever changes in the interface or features.
Google Ads changes its features almost every month.

Many changes affect core functions, not just colors or layout.
Check the account and its settings **regularly**.

A setup that worked a few months ago may behave differently now.
AdWords was renamed Google Ads, and its interface was fully redesigned.

Features may have moved to other menus or may work differently.
So an older guide can send you to settings that no longer exist.

Google has posted over **2,000 changes** to its official AdWords blog in recent years.
Follow the official Google Ads announcements.

Do not rely only on older guides or forum answers.
Build large libraries of campaigns, keywords, audiences and email lists.

Then you can rebuild quickly when Google changes its tools.
A large stock of tested assets is a hedge (protection) against platform changes.
Older guides for conversion tracking setup (the setup that counts sales from ads) often no longer match the current interface and menu names.

Before you follow a guide step by step, check the **actual menus and settings** in the live account.
Compare them with Google's current official documentation.

Platform changes in Google Ads were mainly visible in YouTube campaigns.
So they had limited impact on a standard Shopping setup.

Adjust only when you actually see a change in your own account.
Google Ads changes are not a reason to change a working campaign by themselves.

Shopping layouts shift over time.
A different display on a later check is normal.
Skepticism toward Google recommendations, reps and agencies (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Skepticism toward Google recommendations, reps and agencies
The Google Ads **optimization score** (Google's score of suggested account improvements) should not be treated as actionable advice.

Following Google's recommendations usually means raising budgets and opening up targeting (showing ads to a wider audience).
That can distort the numbers.

Google will call and push budget increases and wide targeting.
Its recommendations generally mean **spending more money**.

Weigh them against your own data.
Google's advice is shaped by its goal of increasing advertiser spend.

Your goal is profit, and the two may differ.
Evaluate every recommendation against your own **margins** (the money left after costs) and results before acting.
If a single keyword wastes about **$100 per week** without producing sales, the usual fix is to pause that keyword.
Google may instead suggest moving it into a Display campaign (ads shown across websites and apps in Google's network), which would keep spend flowing.

Judge that suggestion against your own results.
Applying Google Ads recommendations automatically is risky.

They are generic, auto-generated and not specific to your business.
Only apply a recommendation when you can see a business reason for it.

Do not follow Google's automatic recommendations by default.
This includes one-click auto-apply suggestions.

Apply them only when the account data supports them.
Do not use automatically applied Google Ads recommendations.

Do not follow advice from Google account representatives who call or email the account.
These often add automated spend-raising settings. (2024)

Avoid following Google's advice without checking it.
Changes that raise spend are the **default direction** of its suggestions.
Google Reps
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
Google reps (Google's account managers) often push higher spend.
Treat their recommendation as a sales pitch.

Test changes before committing a large budget.
Google account reps tend to recommend higher budgets, broad targeting and their own suggested campaigns.

These increase spend without improving sales.
Treat their recommendations with caution. (2023)
Reject any agency (an outside firm that runs ads for you) proposal that departs radically from a proven high-ticket Google Ads approach.

Example: broad top-of-funnel targeted search text ads.
Such strategies will not work for high-ticket dropshipping.
Google is a comparison engine and a cost-per-click platform. Cost per click (CPC) is what you pay each time someone clicks.
So your product page is judged against competitors on **price**, title, reviews and delivery.
Relevance (how closely your ad matches the search) and **CTR** (click-through rate: the share of people who see your ad and click it) drive Ad Rank and cost per click.

So **clickable ads** come before higher bids.
Google is strong at the bottom of the funnel (people ready to buy) and the middle (people still comparing).

It is weak at the top of the funnel.
So treat it as a **demand-capture** channel: it catches people who are already looking.

Google Ads is a self-serve pay-per-click platform.
Self-serve means you run it yourself, with no sales call needed.

Pay-per-click (PPC) means you pay only when someone clicks.
Anyone can open an account, set up ads, and change or delete anything without contacting Google.

It was called AdWords until **July 2018**, when it was renamed.
With paid search you pay only when someone clicks.

You control bids, the search terms you appear for, and how your ad looks.
This makes results easier to track and control than organic or unpaid content.
What Google Ads Is (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
Paid search reaches people who are actively looking for a product or solving a problem.
Social feeds are different: people scroll there without asking for anything.
Search intent is the key reason to buy clicks for purchase-ready keywords (words people type when they are ready to buy).

Google paid traffic is generally higher quality and more consistent than social media traffic.
Shoppers actively search for products.
Once an account is set up and working, its performance tends to be more predictable and reliable.
Google works more like a **pull channel** than Meta, Instagram or TikTok.
A pull channel means people come looking for you. A push channel means ads reach people who did not ask.
Meta, Instagram and TikTok mostly push products to people who did not ask for them, which favors impulse buys (quick, unplanned purchases).
On Google, shoppers already look for the product, so results depend on matching existing demand.
Google Ads and Google Shopping attract buyers who search for the specific high-ticket products being sold.

Target customers who are actively searching for the exact product type sold.
They are ready to buy when they reach the site.
A 2018 source says the Google Display Network (Google's group of websites and apps that show its banner ads) reached about **80%** of US internet users.

Google's ad revenue for 2017 was close to **$100 billion**.
This shows that pay-per-click advertising is its main revenue source.
In 2018, on most search result pages for e-commerce keywords (product search words), ads took over more than **50%** of the visible screen.

Often only one organic placement (a free result) was shown.
This indicates Google prioritizes shopping and ad placements for product-related searches.
Google Ads versus other paid channels
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Google Ads (ads shown on Google search and partner websites) is generally **cheaper over the long term** than

Facebook and TikTok ads.
Facebook and TikTok face frequent rule changes, suspensions (account bans) and account problems.

This makes Google a stronger choice for a steady paid channel.
Google Ads needs more knowledge at the start than Facebook Ads.
Give yourself **time to learn it**, because rushing in without that learning often leads to frustration.
Each time someone searches, Google runs an auction (a ranking of advertisers for that search).

Your bid is the highest price you will pay for one click.
Your cost per click (CPC: what you actually pay for one click) usually lands **slightly below your own bid**.
It usually lands above the bid of the advertiser directly below you.

Some advertisers in neighboring positions pay less than their own bid, so the result can vary.
Ads are shown in positions **one to eight** on the results page.
Ad Rank is the score that sets your position. In the example below, it is your bid times your Quality Score.

Bidders whose Ad Rank is too low to reach that range do not appear on the page at all.
Ads shown off the page receive no clicks.

So a low Ad Rank means **lost traffic**, even when the budget is available.
**Worked auction example**:
1. Bidder A has a bid of $4.00 and Quality Score 8, giving Ad Rank 32.
2. The bidder directly below has a bid of $3.45 and Quality Score 7, giving Ad Rank 24.15. This bidder sets the price.

3. Divide 24.15 by 8 and add one cent: about **$3.03** per click, close to the stated $3.02.
**Low-bid example**:

A bidder at $0.50 with a very high Quality Score, in a low slot, paid **$0.19** per click.
The reason: the bidder just below was bidding $0.20.
A high Quality Score can keep costs low even at a small bid.
Quality Score and CTR
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Quality Score is Google's rating of your ad's quality and relevance.

CTR (click-through rate: the share of people who see your ad and click it) is the biggest part of Quality Score.
So **CTR is the first thing to improve**.

Landing page relevance (how closely the page people land on matches the ad) is a pass-or-fail check.
It only needs to be relevant enough to pass.
Keyword relevance means the keyword (the search word you target) must match the ad.

The ad must also match the other keywords in the same ad group (a set of keywords that share ads).
All keywords and the ad should relate closely to each other.

In an account, Quality Scores below **6** are a major problem that should be fixed first.
Such scores usually mean the ads pay penalties on every click.
Higher CTR lowers your cost per click, because Google treats more-clicked ads as more relevant.
That raises **return on ad spend** (ROAS: money earned for each dollar spent on ads). -

**Case: client account, Google Ads, June 29 to July 19**. The team did not change the landing page or anything else. It only worked on **raising CTR**.
**Quality Score**

June 29: 4.7
July 19: 7.5
Change: up 60%
**CTR**
June 29: 5.6%

July 19: 11.65%
Change: roughly doubled
**Cost per click**
June 29: $1.70
July 19: $1.29

Change: down 24.6%
The same traffic cost much less.
The source states the **24.6%** drop.
The rounded prices ($1.70 and $1.29) give about 24.1%, so the stated figure probably comes from unrounded values.
Ad Types
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: **Shopping**
What the source says: Shows product image, price and store name on the results page, so buyers see the offer before clicking. This pre-qualifies clicks and keeps non-buyers from paying for visits.
**Shopping benchmark**
What the source says: A 2015 talk reported Shopping ads convert about 30% better than text ads and produce an average order value about 39% higher.

Treat this as a benchmark for that period, not a guarantee.
**Product Listing Ads (PLAs; Shopping ads that show each product)**
What the source says: Google's Shopping ad format for e-commerce. Optimizing them is a separate skill from running standard search campaigns.
**Search text ads (plain written ads on Google search)**
What the source says: Built on keywords for people actively searching for a solution. Too expensive to generate meaningful volume from completely unaware or problem-aware audiences.

**Display retargeting (showing ads again to past visitors)**
What the source says: Dynamic retargeting and general retargeting.
**YouTube, Display and Gmail (cold) (cold means people who do not know you yet)**
What the source says: Top-of-funnel.
Targets in-market users (people actively looking to buy something like this) and demographics (age, location and similar traits) that resemble website visitors and customers.

Sends traffic to a non-commercial page (a page that does not try to sell directly).
**Performance Max (Google's automated campaign type)**
What the source says: Start with Shopping and Performance Max only after the data supports it.
Funnel position: bottom, middle and top
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: The funnel is the set of steps a buyer goes through, from not knowing you to buying.
It has three stages: top, middle and bottom.
Pay-per-click (PPC: you pay only when someone clicks) ads should send the **right traffic, at the right time, at the right price** to your website.
This applies to every paid traffic source, including Google Ads, Facebook ads, banner ads (picture ads on websites) and Pinterest ads.
Ads do not have to produce the conversion themselves. A conversion is when a visitor takes the wanted action, usually a purchase.

The right traffic is a person who is in the market for your product at some point and matches your ideal customer.
They may not be ready to buy today.

In Google Ads, this means a search with relevant intent (what the searcher wants) toward the products you sell.
Not every searcher is the right traffic.
Right time refers to the customer's position in the sales funnel, not your own schedule.
Top-of-funnel users do not yet know what they need, so buy-focused ads aimed at bottom-of-funnel users will not make sense to them.
Match the ad message to where the person is in the funnel: **top, middle or bottom**.
Google Shopping works well for prospects who are most aware of their need or already know the product.
It is poorly suited to prospects who are only aware of their problem.
It usually sends visitors to a product page, which often does not move a problem-aware visitor forward.
Paid search text ads can become too expensive to generate meaningful volume from completely unaware or problem-aware audiences.
They are better suited to prospects who are **actively searching for a solution**.
If targeting (choosing who sees your ads) is weak, the offer and site presentation are much less likely to convert, even if they are strong.
Targeting does not have to hold the highest single share of conversion chances to be critical.
Getting the audience right is necessary for the rest of the funnel to succeed.
Campaign build order
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Campaign build order for a paid search funnel, from highest to lowest priority:
1. Audience-based search campaigns (ads aimed at people already known to you or similar), starting with bottom-of-funnel priorities.
2. Shopping ads with stacked targeting (several targeting layers combined), including retargeting, serving shopping ads to people who previously visited the website.
3. Search text ads with stacked targeting on the winning keywords learned from shopping campaigns, so shopping results inform the search text ad keywords.
4. Display retargeting: dynamic retargeting and general retargeting.
5. Search campaigns without audiences (cold traffic, meaning people who do not know you), including shopping campaigns to cold traffic.
6. Middle-of-funnel audience search text campaigns to cold traffic, targeting people looking for information related to the products, such as buyer's guides or comparison guides.
7. Top-of-funnel cold traffic on display, YouTube and Gmail, targeting in-market users and demographics that resemble website visitors and customers, sent to a non-commercial page.
Source C advises against running standard Google search campaigns for a product store.

The reason: cost per click is very high, even though search generates a lot of traffic.
Use shopping-based campaigns instead.

This applies to the early setup of a product store.
Source A says search campaigns have a place once a store is scaling (growing big), but not in the first stage.

Start with Shopping and Performance Max only after the data supports it.
Source A's build order places search after shopping and retargeting.

Cold search without audiences comes at step 5.
Both sources agree that search is **not the first step**.

Source C's warning applies to standard search in a product store's early setup.
Source A's sequence applies once shopping and retargeting data exist.
When Google suits a product or store
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: Before adopting a Google Ads strategy, check which business type it was built for.
A tactic that works for one model, such as a law firm or a high-margin service (margin is the profit left after costs), may not work for a low-margin high-ticket dropshipping store.

Dropshipping means you sell products that a supplier ships to the buyer.
High-ticket means expensive products.
Always weigh the price of the product against what each click costs.
Some Google Shopping tactics work for low-ticket products (cheap products), because buyers face little risk and purchase quickly.

The same tactics often fail for high-ticket products.
Using the wrong tactic for your business type wastes both time and ad budget.
For a high-ticket dropshipping store, Google Ads is usually **the first paid traffic source** to build, ahead of other channels.

It remains a core part of the overall marketing system afterward.
A typical Google Ads setup for a high-ticket dropshipping store combines three parts:

Google Shopping campaigns.
Search text ad campaigns.
Display network retargeting campaigns (ads on partner websites, shown to past visitors).
Business buyers search Google the same way consumers do, so target them with the same Google Ads setup.
Also place banner ads on trade and industry websites that business buyers visit.

Shoppers compare Google Shopping listings that show near-identical photos and descriptions.
So price is often the only factor for the first click.

Matching the **lowest price** is needed to earn that click.
Undercutting (selling just below rivals' prices) causes a price war where everyone loses.

Competing with Amazon works best with non-US stores.
Amazon has about **80%** market share in the US (the share of the market it controls).

Local markets where Amazon is weaker offer more room.
A non-US store requires more effort to find suppliers, often about **two extra weeks**.
Before choosing a Google campaign type, check whether you are building your own brand or running a dropshipping-style store.
That decides how much differentiation (making your product look different from others) the product needs.
Brand-building stores should move to their own designs and photos once a tested product shows demand.
Mindset: the ad is not the sales tool
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t:
Thinking that a good ad alone causes sales is a common error.
It leads to lower profitability (less profit) and wasted spend.

Evaluate ads by the clicks and visitor quality they produce.
Also check whether the site turns that traffic into profit.
Google account reps (the Google staff assigned to your account) push more spend and services,

such as search campaigns, that are not needed at the start.
Follow the account data and the blueprint instead of their upsell advice (pitches to buy more).
When judging a PPC agency (a company that runs pay-per-click ads for you) or freelancer, assess three areas.

Check **activity**: current account work and recent results.
Check **communication**: response speed and clear, regular output.

Check **technical expertise**: depth of paid search knowledge.
Use these as a screening checklist, not as a guarantee of results.
Google ranks agencies on performance and customer care.
So a Google Partner status (Google's official agency badge) with a top-tier standing is one signal of an agency's recent activity.
Verify the status directly in **Google's partner directory** before relying on it.
A WordStream study ranks advertisers on performance, customer care and account activity.

A **top 5%** placement is cited as a benchmark (a yardstick) for a strong account.
The figure is a vendor claim (a claim made by the seller).

Confirm it against the study itself before using it as a hiring criterion.
A PPC-only agency tends to have deeper technical expertise than a generalist agency.

The reason: the team builds its strategies from years of paid search work.
When vetting one, ask how long they have run PPC and whether paid search is their only service.
Agencies, reps and outsourcing (continued)
p.s: How Google Ads works and where it fits

p.t: When screening a PPC agency for a store, ask whether they have managed PLA campaigns specifically.
Do not accept general AdWords accounts (the old name for Google Ads) as proof.
Ad agencies that cold-email newly created Shopify stores (Shopify is an online store platform) usually sign up many clients without improving results.
Do not pay an outside agency until the owner has made ads **profitable**.
Set up Google Ads yourself first, and get them to at least profitable before considering an outside service.

Outsourcing (hiring outside help) comes after the owner knows what works.
A Google Ads ROAS of **3.26** was reported at one point.
The account was outsourced to an agency after the speaker had set it up.
Product-focused Google ads that send buyers straight to product pages should be used first.
The reason: those people already want to buy.

Lead generation ads (ads that collect contact details from interested people) need more money, content and time to pay off.
So they are a later addition.
1. **Learn** the theory of pay-per-click advertising and the buyer psychology (why buyers act) behind search campaigns.
2. **Set up and launch** the Google Ads and Google Shopping campaigns so they start generating traffic.
3. **Move into** a management phase, where ongoing monitoring and adjustment of campaigns is the main source of learning.
